name: Vacuum
frequency: Reference value; ideal vacuum is frequency-independent in the basic model
description: Vacuum is the reference medium used to define relative permittivity. Its relative permittivity is exactly 1 by definition in the elementary model.

name: Air (dry, near sea level)
loss: Very low; often treated as ≈ 0 in introductory tables
frequency: Reference value; depends slightly on pressure, humidity and frequency
description: Dry air has a relative permittivity very close to 1. It is commonly used as an insulating medium in capacitors and electrical equipment.

name: PTFE (Teflon)
description: PTFE is a low-loss polymer dielectric used in high-frequency cables, connectors and insulation.
source: ScienceDirect insulating-material table; NI capacitor reference

name: Polyethylene
description: Polyethylene is a low-permittivity, low-loss insulating polymer commonly used for wire and cable insulation.

name: Mica
description: Mica is a layered mineral with good insulating properties and relatively low dielectric loss. It is used in capacitors and electrical insulation.

name: Soda-lime glass
description: Soda-lime glass is an inorganic dielectric. Its electrical properties vary with composition, temperature and test frequency.

name: Alumina ceramic
description: Alumina is a ceramic dielectric used in electronic substrates, insulators and component packages. The loss depends strongly on purity and grade.
source: ScienceDirect dielectric-materials table; recent electronic-packaging review

name: Dry paper
description: Dry paper is a cellulose-based dielectric. Moisture can significantly increase its permittivity and dielectric loss; the value is for dry paper.

name: Bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde)
description: Bakelite is a thermosetting resin historically used for electrical switches, plugs and insulating components. Formulation and filler change its properties.

name: Polystyrene
description: Polystyrene is a low-loss thermoplastic dielectric used in insulation and some capacitor applications.
